title: Codify postmortem actions into verifiable shipping contracts for runtime degradations
creator: Lena Park
description:
Summary: After the Feb 2026 KV-cache regeneration incident (postmortem link below), we need a compact, auditable set of PRD requirements that translate the postmortem action items into minimal shippable contracts. These contracts will be the gating criteria for runtime changes (kernels/quantization/autoscale) and deployment rollouts so that future regressions are prevented or mitigated automatically.

Objectives:
- Convert high-level postmortem items into discrete requirements with owners, test vectors, and verification steps.
- Define rollout gates and automatic fallback/rollback triggers tied to observable signals and SLO thresholds.
- Specify a verifiable acceptance harness (synthetic tests + CI checks + dashboard verification) so product, eng, and SRE can sign-off.
- Ensure requirements are implementable in phases: quick wins for this quarter + follow-up medium-term items.

Why this now: Multiple recent incidents exposed gaps between postmortem actions and what actually ships. We need a deterministic way to ensure postmortem mitigations are present in future PRDs and enforced during rollout, not just listed in the incident.
scope: In scope: 1) PRD sections that codify postmortem actions as acceptance contracts; 2) mapping of SLO/metric thresholds to specific automated runbook/rollback behaviors; 3) a small synthetic verification harness and CI gating plan; 4) dashboard spec and ownership. Out of scope: re-architecting the serving runtime, replacing core KV-cache implementation, or building a fully automated incident-response system in this cycle.
acceptance_criteria: Every postmortem action referenced in the Feb 2026 KV-cache incident has a corresponding PRD requirement clause with an owner and implementation notes.
For each PRD requirement, there is at least one deterministic verification step: synthetic job, CI test, or dashboard KPI that can be checked automatically.
Rollout gating rules are specified for canary->gradual rollout with clear thresholds that trigger an automatic rollback or fallback to a compatible model variant.
Automated runbook snippets are drafted for the top three failure modes (KV-cache regen stalls, cold-start autoscale failure, memory regression) and included as appendices to the PRD.
A lightweight acceptance harness is added to the runtime-1.20 release pipeline that runs synthetic checks; it must pass 3 consecutive runs before a canary can graduate.
Dashboards list the SLOs, their mapped actions, and the owner; on-call has a one-click link to trigger the documented fallback policy.
Stakeholder sign-off: product, infra eng, SRE, and security (if required) have approved the PRD acceptance section.
Documentation: links to the incident postmortem, implementation RFCs, and PRs are embedded in the PRD and tracked in this ticket.
decisions: Adopt a phased approach: Phase A (this cycle) will cover the top 3 mitigations with deterministic checks; Phase B will expand to remaining actions and automation.
Verification priority: synthetic + CI checks first, full automation of runbook execution deferred to Phase B.
Rollback semantics: define an automatic rollback for canary when error rate > 1.5% AND latency p95 increases by >30% sustained for 5 minutes.
Owner model: product owns the PRD requirement, engineering owns implementation, SRE owns runbook verification and dashboards.
tradeoffs: We prioritize fast, verifiable controls over perfect automation this cycle. That means some mitigations will be manual with clear playbooks rather than fully automated—this reduces scope and delivery risk but increases operational burden until Phase B. Avoids risky infra changes during a high-velocity release window.
